title: What founders should expect from a Next.js company site
metaTitle: A Next.js marketing website, in practice
excerpt: A Next.js marketing website should give you a fast public site, a repository you own, and a clear place to edit content. The framework name is not the outcome.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp. The screens fit a piece about what a company site looks like when it is actually built.
caption: What you should expect is a site you can open, read, and own. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a founder expect from a Next.js site?
faqs.answer: A fast public site, a repository in an account you own, and a place to change the words without a scavenger hunt. You should be able to see the pages on a staging address before launch, and you should know who can deploy. The framework is the means. Those three outcomes are the expectation.

faqs.question: Do I need to understand React to own the site?
faqs.answer: You need to understand what you own and how to get help. You do not need to write components on day one. You do need the repository, the host account, and the content logins in your name. A future developer, in-house or not, should be able to open the project and find the pages.

faqs.question: Is Next.js only for web applications?
faqs.answer: No. It is a reasonable way to build a company site that is mostly read, with a few dynamic parts such as a form, a blog, or an account later. A brochure can be static pages. The value is the same team can add a product interface without throwing the marketing site away.

markdown:
A Next.js marketing website should feel, to a founder, like three concrete things. A public site that loads as a finished page. A repository you own and can hand to another developer. A place where the words and images live so a Tuesday edit does not require a rebuild of the layout. The framework's name is not the benefit. Those three are.

Skip the trivia. You do not need a tour of rendering modes to decide whether the project succeeded. You need to know what you can open, what you can change, and what happens when someone on a phone hits the homepage.

## A fast public site

Expect the homepage, the work, and the contact path to arrive as readable HTML, not as a blank screen waiting on a large script. A company site is opened by strangers, once, often on a phone. If the first view depends on an application booting, you built a product shell for a page that wanted to be a page.

Google's [Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) give you the numbers to ask for, without a framework debate. A good Largest Contentful Paint is within 2.5 seconds. A good Interaction to Next Paint is 200 milliseconds or less. A good Cumulative Layout Shift is 0.1 or less. The recommendation is to judge the 75th percentile of loads, on mobile and desktop, not the best demo on the office wifi. Next.js can help you get there, because pages can be built ahead of time and shipped as static files. It will not get you there if every page is a client application wearing a marketing layout.

Hanabi uses Next.js for the public site for that reason. The marketing pages stay static where they can. The result a founder should notice is not the badge. It is a page that is already words when it appears.

## A repository you own

Expect the code in a repository under your account, not a studio's private folder that you are allowed to look at. Expect a README that says how to run it and how to deploy it. Expect the host, such as Vercel, in an account your company controls. If the only copy of the site lives in someone else's login, you have a subscription to a vendor, not a website.

The stack around a Hanabi build is the one you should be able to name in a sentence if you want to. Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind for the interface. The names matter less than the fact that a competent developer outside the original project can read them. Exotic tooling that only one contractor understands is a lock-in, even when the repository is technically yours.

You should be able to see a staging URL before anything touches the real domain. Staging is where you read the pages, click the form, and decide the launch is real. A surprise on production is a failure of the handoff, not a property of the framework.

## A place for the content

Expect an answer to the question of who changes the headline. Sometimes the answer is a developer, in a file, because the page changes rarely and the structure is fixed. Sometimes the answer is an editor in a CMS, because a marketing person will publish often. Both are legitimate. What is not legitimate is a shrug, or a page builder layered on top until nobody knows which version is true.

Hanabi keeps its own articles in Payload, separate from the client portal that holds brand files and project updates. That split is a useful picture even if your stack differs. The public words have an editor and a draft. The private delivery files have a door. A company site should be able to explain its version of the split. Blog here. Landing pages there. The thing customers never see somewhere else.

If you are the person who will edit, sit in that tool before you accept the build. Change a sentence on staging. Preview it. Publish it, or ask for it to be published, and see the live page. A CMS demo with sample latin is not the test. Your headline is the test.

## What you should not expect

Do not expect the framework to supply a brand, a message, or a structure. Next.js will render whatever hierarchy you hand it, including a vague one. The pages a stranger needs are still a decision: what this is, why it is credible, how to talk to a person.

Do not expect every future idea to be a new dependency. A form, a blog, and a simple account can belong. A plugin for every campaign idea will recreate the mess people were leaving behind. The advantage of a codebase is that you can say no to a plugin and write the one thing you need, or refuse the feature.

Do not expect magic speed. Images that are larger than the layout, fonts that block rendering, and third-party scripts for tools you barely use will make a Next.js site slow. Ask what the page is requesting. The framework will not cancel a tag someone pasted into the head.

## How to review the project without learning the framework

Read the site as a customer. Then look at ownership as an operator.

- Can you find the offer in the first screen, on a phone?
- Does the primary action respond without a visible stall?
- Is the repository in your account, and can someone else run it from the README?
- Can the headline change without a treasure hunt?
- Do you control the domain and the host login?

If those are true, the framework choice is doing its job. If they are false, a different framework would not have saved you. The gap is in the agreement about what done means.

The content place is the decision people postpone, and then regret. [Choosing a CMS when the marketing team is small](/blog/choosing-a-cms) is the next piece. It asks who edits, how often, and whether drafts matter.

When you want that kind of company site designed and built, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The expectation is a fast public site, in a repository you own, with a clear place for the words.
